title: Our method in each style
teaches: The same steps run every trade, day, swing or position: find the setup, set the stop, size from it, manage it, review it, under our 2% ceiling. What changes with the clock is the chart you read, where the stop sits and so the size, and whether you carry gaps overnight.

walkthroughs.title: Same steps, any clock
steps: Same steps on any clock: find the setup, set the stop, size from it, manage it, review it.
That holds whether you're out by the close or holding for months.
What changes is the chart you read, where the stop sits, and so the size.
With a winner, we sell partials into strength and trail the rest under the rising averages.

walkthroughs.title: What our rules set
steps: Some things never change with the clock. We risk 0.25% to 2% of the account a trade. 2% is the ceiling.
The stop goes a few cents under the low of the day, or the prior day's low.
The first sell is a judgment. We very rarely sell on day 1, and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest.

walkthroughs.title: What changes with the clock
steps: A short-term trader buying near the open might put the stop under the low of the first 10 minutes.
A longer-term trader judges exits on a longer chart, so the stop sits farther away.
Put the stop where it belongs and change the size. Wider stop, fewer shares, same risk.

questions.q: You've only swing traded and want to try a few day trades. What can you leave out of the plan?
choices: The size, it's only a few hours
The exit, you're out by the close
questions.why: Nothing. A day trade is the same trade on a shorter clock. You still write down the entry, the stop, the size and the exit before you click buy. Watching the screen isn't a stop. Every position gets a real stop order with the broker, because a fast market can blow through your price before you react. And being out by the close is a deadline, not an exit. You still need the price that tells you you're wrong. We swing trade, so day trades are rare for us. When you take one, the plan doesn't get thinner.
questions.lesson_line: A shorter hold is no excuse for a thinner plan.

wrong.The stop, you'll be watching: Watching isn't a stop. Put a real stop order in with the broker. In a fast market the price is gone before you click.
wrong.The size, it's only a few hours: The size is what caps the loss. It comes from the dollars you'll risk over the distance to your stop, whatever the clock.
wrong.The exit, you're out by the close: The close is a deadline, not an exit. You still need the price that says you're wrong.

questions.simple: Nothing, because a day trade still needs a stop, a size and an exit. Only the clock gets shorter.

reasons: fixed before (key reworded by the checker)

questions.q: You'll be out of a day trade by the close, so it can risk more than 2% of the account.
questions.why: False. 2% of the account is the most we risk on any trade, day trade or swing. Our risk runs 0.25% to 2%, picked by the setup, your recent results, the market and your edge. How long you plan to hold isn't on that list. And being out by the close doesn't cap the loss. A stop is only a trigger, and a fast market can fill it well below your price. So the day trade gets the same ceiling, and most of the time a lot less.
questions.lesson_line: 2% is the ceiling in every style. The clock doesn't raise it.
questions.simple: False, because 2% is the most we ever risk on one trade, and a short hold doesn't change what can go wrong.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A1, 2% ceiling)

questions.q: You spot a setup you like. What order do you work the trade in?
questions.why: Setup, stop, size, manage, review. The setup comes first, because the stop goes where that setup breaks. Then you measure from your entry to the stop, and only then do you size. The size comes from the stop, never the other way around. Pick a size first and you end up squeezing the stop to fit it, right into the normal noise. Then you manage the trade. And after you're out, you review it. The trade isn't done when you sell.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, then size. The order never changes, only the clock does.

wrong.Setup, size, stop, manage, review: Size before stop is the classic mistake. You can't size until you know how far away the stop is.
wrong.Size, setup, stop, manage, review: That picks a size before there's even a setup. The stop ends up bent around the size.
wrong.Stop, setup, size, manage, review: The stop goes where the setup fails, so you need the setup first. A stop picked before the chart isn't tied to anything.

questions.simple: Setup, stop, size, manage, review, because the size comes from how far away the stop is.

reasons: fixed before (f19 added by the checker)

questions.q: Tap the word that fits.
questions.sentence: Same stock, same risk, wider stop: the position gets ___.
questions.why: Smaller. Shares are the dollars you'll risk divided by the distance to the stop. Move the stop farther away and the same risk buys fewer shares.
questions.lesson_line: The chart sets the stop. The stop sets the size.

questions.q: You and a friend buy at the same price, same stop. He'll hold for months, you for days. Your 3R price is the same as his.
questions.why: True. R is your risk per share, the entry minus the stop. 3R is three of those added to the entry. So it's a price on the chart, not a date. Same entry, same stop, same 3R, however long either of you holds. What really moves 3R is the stop. A longer hold often runs a wider stop, and that pushes 3R farther out. And 3R is a mark, not a sell order. We very rarely sell on day 1, and the first sell is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: R is measured from the stop, not from the calendar.
questions.simple: True, because the 3R price comes from the entry and the stop. How long you hold doesn't move it.

deeper.trap: The catch is the stop, not the clock. Longer holds often use wider stops, and a wider stop pushes 3R farther from the entry. This question fixes the entry and the stop, so the 3R price matches. Change the stop and the price moves with it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)

questions.q: A Go Signal: the stock opened weak and trades back up through yesterday's close. You buy on the 30-minute chart. Where's your stop?
choices: Just under the low of the day
questions.answer: Just under the low of the day
questions.why: A few cents under the low of the day, the LOD. That's where the Go Signal stop lives. The stock dipped to that low, buyers stepped in, and it turned back up through yesterday's close. If it takes out the LOD, the turn failed and you're wrong. Timing the buy on the 30-minute chart gets you a cleaner entry. It doesn't move the stop onto that clock. Put it a few cents under, not right on the low, so a tick to the exact low doesn't take you out.
questions.lesson_line: Time the buy on the 30-minute if you like. The stop stays under the low of the day.

wrong.Under the last 30-minute bar: That puts the stop on your entry's clock. One normal wiggle inside the day takes you out before the idea is wrong.
wrong.A flat 10% under your buy: A flat percent isn't tied to anything on the chart. The chart already shows where you're wrong, the LOD.
wrong.Just under yesterday's close: That's your entry level, so there's no room at all. The stock was trading under it this morning.

questions.simple: Just under the low of the day, because that's where the turn fails, whatever chart you time the buy on.

reasons: rests on house plans (TRADE_PLANS.md Go Signal) and the rulebook (F62)
key reworded for length balance and F62

questions.q: You're a day trader, so you never hold through a gap. That means your stop always fills right at your stop price.
questions.why: False. A stop price is a trigger, not a promise. When it's hit, it turns into a market order and you get the next price there is. In a fast market that can be well under your stop, in the middle of the day, no gap needed. Skipping overnight holds takes away one risk. It doesn't take away this one. So plan like the fill can be worse than the stop. That's one more reason a tight stop never earns you a giant position.
questions.lesson_line: A stop is a trigger, not a guaranteed price. In every style.
questions.simple: False, because a stop only triggers a market order, and in a fast market that order can fill well below your stop.

deeper.trap: A short intraday drop can trigger a stop and fill it far below where the stock closes that day. So a day trader can lose more than planned with no gap at all. The SEC calls the stop price a trigger, not the execution price.

questions.q: You swing trade most of the time and take a day trade now and then. Which of these changes between the two?
questions.why: Where your stop sits. Know your timeframe on every trade, because it decides where you're wrong. Someone buying near the open might put the stop under the low of the first 10 minutes. On our swing trades it's a few cents under the low of the day or the prior day's low. A longer-term trader judges exits on a longer chart still. Move the stop and the size moves with it, for the same risk. The 2% ceiling, the written plan and the review never change.
questions.lesson_line: Know your timeframe on every trade. It tells you where the stop goes.

wrong.Our 2% risk ceiling: That one never moves. 2% is the most we risk on any trade, day trade or swing.
wrong.Having a written plan: Every style needs one. A day trader still plans the entry, the exit and the risk.
wrong.Reviewing your trades: Every trade gets reviewed, whatever the clock. You don't learn from trades you never look at.

questions.simple: Where your stop sits, because each clock has its own spot where you're wrong. The ceiling, the plan and the review don't change.

questions.q: Day trade, $50,000 account. You buy at $18.60 with the stop at $18.35, under the first 10-minute low. You'll risk $200. How many shares?
questions.why: 800 shares. Same math as your swing trades. $18.60 minus $18.35 is 0.25, so you risk 25 cents a share. $200 divided by 0.25 is 800. Then check the cap. 800 shares at $18.60 stays well under 40% of the $50,000 account, so the size stands. The tight stop is why the share count looks big. That's fine, because your loss at the stop is still the $200 you planned.
questions.lesson_line: Day trade or swing, shares are the dollars you risk over the risk per share.
questions.simple: 800 shares, because you divide the $200 you risk by the distance from your entry to your stop.

reasons: fixed before (stem reworded by the checker)

wrong.1,075 shares: That fills the 40% cap instead of sizing from the $200 risk. The cap is a ceiling, not a target.
wrong.2,688 shares: That's the whole $50,000 spent at $18.60. Your size comes from the risk, not from what the account can buy.
wrong.8,000 shares: A decimal slip, ten times too many. $200 over 0.25 is 800.

questions.q: A friend wants to hold a stock for up to a year. Which of these gives him the best read on the trend?
questions.why: The 200-day. Match the average to how long you hold. A 9 EMA hugs price and turns the moment price turns. That's what we want on a swing trade that lasts days to weeks. On a hold of up to a year it would shake him out of every normal pullback. For a hold that long, the 200-day gives the better read. We watch it too, as a line, not as our trail. We don't buy stocks under the 200-day. That's a hard line. Our swing trades still trail under the 9 or 20 EMA.
questions.lesson_line: Match the average to the clock. Short hold, short line. Long hold, long line.

wrong.The 100-hour average: That's 100 bars, but hourly ones. A year-long hold needs a daily line, not intraday levels.
wrong.The 9 EMA: That's a swing trader's line. It hugs price and turns fast, so a long hold gets shaken out on a normal dip.
wrong.The 20 EMA: Better than the 9, still too short. We trail under it for days to weeks, not a year.

questions.simple: The 200-day, because a long hold needs a long average. A short one would shake you out of every pullback.

deeper.counter: Not every long-term trader uses the 200-day. ChartSchool only says long-term investors often use 100 or more periods. The point is the match: a short average for a short hold, a long one for a long hold.

reasons: touches the rulebook's E52 trail (owner flag)

questions.q: You buy a Go Signal as it trades back through yesterday's $40.00 close. Stop at $39.20. Where's your 3R mark?
questions.why: $42.40. $40.00 minus $39.20 is 0.80, so you risk 80 cents a share. That's 1R. Three times 0.80 is 2.40. Add it to $40.00 and you get $42.40. Mark it on the chart, but it's a mark, not a sell order. The first sell is a judgment. We very rarely sell on day 1, and we mostly wait until day 3 at the earliest.
questions.lesson_line: 3R is a mark on the chart, not a sell order.
questions.simple: $42.40, because your risk is the entry minus the stop, and 3R adds three of those to the entry.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)
fixed before (2R target moved to 3R trim)

wrong.$43.00: That's a flat $3.00 on top, not three times your risk.
wrong.$41.60: That's 2R. You added two times the 0.80, not three.
wrong.$44.00: That's five times your risk on top, not three.

questions.story: You plan a position trade in a US stock and expect to hold it about six months. The entry, stop and size are written down.
questions.q: What does this plan still need that a day trade plan can skip?
choices: What you'll do at each report
The low of the first 10 minutes
Which hourly bar you'll buy on
questions.answer: What you'll do at each report
questions.why: What you'll do at each report. US companies report every quarter, so six months means sitting through earnings. News outside trading hours can gap the stock right past your stop. In Fidelity's example a stop at 95 sold near 90 after an overnight gap. So decide before you buy. Our rule: hold through a report only if you're up 5R. And no new buys in the 3 days before a report, in any style. A day trade is flat by the close, so it never has to make that call.
questions.lesson_line: A long hold sits through earnings. Decide what you'll do before you buy.

wrong.Nothing, the stop covers it: A gap can jump the stop. In Fidelity's example a stop at 95 sold near 90.
wrong.The low of the first 10 minutes: That's a stop for a quick trade near the open. A six-month hold judges exits on a much longer chart.
wrong.Which hourly bar you'll buy on: Every trade picks its entry. Your entry bar does nothing when a report gaps the stock.

questions.simple: What you'll do at each report, because a six-month hold sits through earnings, and a gap can jump your stop.

reasons: fixed before (story gave the key away)

questions.q: You only make a few position trades a year. With so few, there's no real need to journal and review them.
questions.why: False. Fewer trades is more reason to review, not less. Each one carries more weight, and you get fewer chances to learn. Closing the trade isn't the last step. Log it in your journal the same day, and go over the week every weekend, ideally. Keep good records so you can actually see whether you're getting better. Without them you're just guessing.
questions.lesson_line: Every style ends the same way. Log it, then review it.
questions.simple: False, because every trade gets journaled and reviewed, and with only a few a year, each one teaches you more.

questions.story: You hold two swing trades and have a few new buys lined up for this week. Then the general market turns weak and most stocks start falling.
questions.q: What's the play from here?
choices: Take fewer new trades for now
Ignore it, the stock is what counts
Widen your stops to ride it out
Buy more, prices are lower now
questions.answer: Take fewer new trades for now
questions.why: Take fewer new trades. When the market turns, good setups fail more often because the market isn't backing them. Our market filter, the app's Green, Yellow, Orange and Red reading, sets how much we trade. As it weakens it's fewer and smaller trades, then only the best, and in Red mostly cash. Your two open trades keep their stops. A stop only moves up, never down or wider. Let the market earn your exposure back.
questions.lesson_line: When the market turns weak, trade less. Let it earn your exposure back.

wrong.Ignore it, the stock is what counts: Most stocks go with the market. Trade against it and good setups fail through no fault of their own.
wrong.Widen your stops to ride it out: That's more risk right as the market turns on you. A stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Buy more, prices are lower now: That's adding to a loser. We buy the full size once, at one price, and never add to a loser, least of all into a falling market.

questions.simple: Take fewer new trades, because a weak market makes good setups fail more often. Your open trades keep their stops.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A1 market conditions, A4 stop only moves up)

questions.q: Jeffrey Hirsch holds longer term with stops as wide as 20%, but never lets one position cost over 2% of the portfolio. Max position?
questions.why: 10% of the portfolio. 2 divided by 20 is 0.1, so 10%. Check it. A 10% position that drops 20% costs you 2% of the portfolio, right at his cap. That's how a wide stop works on a long hold. The stop goes where the trend breaks, and the size shrinks to fit. Our stops sit much tighter, mostly within about 3% of the buy. So for the same risk, our positions can be bigger.
questions.lesson_line: A wide stop is fine on a long hold. The size shrinks so the risk doesn't grow.
questions.simple: 10% of the portfolio, because a 10% position that falls 20% loses 2%, right at his cap.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading the 20% as a stop to copy. It is Hirsch's outer limit for a longer-term portfolio, paired with a small position. A 20% stop on a big position breaks the 2% cap fast. Our own stops usually sit within about 3% of the buy.

wrong.20% of the portfolio: That's the stop width, not the size. A position that big with a 20% stop costs double his cap.
wrong.2% of the portfolio: That's the loss cap, not the position. You'd be sizing way smaller than you need to.
wrong.40% of the portfolio: That multiplies the 2% cap by the 20% stop. Divide them instead.

questions.story: Your day trade is up 2R at 3:45 p.m. and closing strong. You sized it for a tight intraday stop. No earnings are due, and you'd like to hold it a few days.
questions.q: If you hold it overnight, what has to change?
choices: New plan: daily stop, new size
Keep the size, stop to breakeven
Keep the intraday stop and size
questions.answer: New plan: daily stop, new size
questions.why: New plan: daily stop, new size. The trade was built for one day, with a stop for intraday moves. For a hold of days, I'd use our default stop. That is a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low. A wider stop means a smaller size for the same risk. So sell part of it into strength until the size fits. A tight stop never justifies a big position, because a gap can jump the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Change the clock and you re-run the steps: new stop, new size.

wrong.Nothing, it's already working: The plan was built for one day. News after the close can gap it, and the stop was set for intraday moves.
wrong.Keep the size, stop to breakeven: A breakeven stop can't catch an overnight gap, and the size was built for a tight intraday stop. A gap down at that size costs far more than planned.
wrong.Keep the intraday stop and size: A tight intraday stop sits inside a normal day's swings, so a hold of days can get stopped out early. It can't catch an overnight gap either.

questions.simple: Make a new plan with our default daily stop, because a wider stop means a smaller size for the same risk.

deeper.trap: The trap is that a winner feels safe. Being up 2R at 3:45 p.m. says nothing about tonight's news. The size came from a tight intraday stop. An overnight gap at that size can cost far more than the plan allowed. Re-run the steps as if it were a new trade: stop first, then size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (default stop, F62, A7)

questions.story: You and a friend own the same stock. It pulls back to the 50-day, and the long uptrend is intact. Your swing stop gets hit. His position-trade stop sits lower and holds.
questions.q: Which of you broke your plan?
questions.why: Neither of you. You each had a stop built for your own clock. Your swing stop sat close, so this pullback took you out, and selling was the plan. His sat lower, for a hold of months. It wasn't touched, so holding was his plan. If the stock turns back up, you'll feel like you sold too early. If it keeps falling, he'll feel like he held too long. Neither feeling means a plan broke. You break a plan when you skip your own stop.
questions.lesson_line: Judge each trade by its own plan, not by how someone else's turned out.

wrong.Both, the stops should match: Different holds need different stops. Match them and one of you is on the wrong clock.
wrong.Him, for holding on: His stop sits on a longer clock, and this pullback didn't reach it. Holding was his plan.
wrong.You, for selling: Taking your stop was the plan. Holding past it would have been the mistake.

questions.simple: Neither, because each of you followed a stop set for your own clock, and a pullback can hit one without the other.

deeper.trap: The trap is judging one plan by the other's result. If the stock turns back up, the swing trader may feel wrong for selling. If it keeps falling, the position trader may feel wrong for holding. Neither feeling means a plan was broken. A plan is broken when you skip your own stop or rule.

questions.story: You buy a Kicker at $50.00 as it trades through the red day's high. The Kicker day's low is $47.00.
questions.q: Where's your stop?
questions.why: $48.25. On a Kicker the stop goes a few cents under the Kicker day's low, or 3.5% under your entry if that's closer. Work both. 3.5% under $50.00 is $48.25. The $47.00 low is farther down, so the closer one wins. A Kicker is meant to go right away. If it gives back more than 3.5%, it isn't acting like one. A stop way down at $47.00 just costs you more per share for the same idea.
questions.lesson_line: Kicker stop: the candle's low or 3.5%, whichever is closer.

wrong.$45.00, 10% under entry: A flat 10% isn't the Kicker plan. It's the low or 3.5%, whichever is closer.
wrong.Just under the $47.00 low: That's the other half of the rule, and here it's farther away. The closer one wins.
wrong.$48.50, 3% under entry: Close, but the Kicker stop is 3.5%, not 3%. 3.5% under $50.00 is $48.25.

questions.simple: $48.25, because the Kicker stop takes whichever is closer to your buy, and 3.5% under $50.00 beats the $47.00 low.

deeper.trap: The trap is picking the candle's low because it looks like the natural stop. On a big Kicker candle the low can sit far below the entry. The rule takes the closer of the two, so the 3.5% half caps how far below the entry the stop can sit.

reasons: rests on house plans (TRADE_PLANS.md Kicker row)

questions.story: Your day trades put 25% of the account in, with stops 2% under entry. You switch to position trades, keep 25% positions, and set stops 10% under.
questions.q: What just happened to your risk?
choices: Risk is now 2.5%, over our ceiling
Risk fell, the stop is farther away
Risk is now 10%, same as the stop
questions.answer: Risk is now 2.5%, over our ceiling
questions.why: It's now 2.5% of the account, over our 2% ceiling. Risk is size times stop distance. Before, 25% times 2% was 0.5% of the account. Now it's 25% times 10%, which is 2.5%. Same size, five times the stop, five times the risk. To get back under 2%, you shrink the size to fit the wider stop. Change the stop and you re-run the size, every time.
questions.lesson_line: New clock, new stop, new size. Never carry the old size over.

wrong.Risk fell, the stop is farther away: A farther stop means a bigger loss per share. Same size, more risk.
wrong.Risk is now 10%, same as the stop: 10% is what the position loses, not the account. 25% times 10% is 2.5%.
wrong.Nothing, the size didn't change: The unchanged size is the problem. The stop got five times wider, so the risk did too.

questions.simple: Risk is now 2.5%, because a 25% position with a 10% stop risks 2.5% of the account, over our ceiling.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking the position size alone is the risk. The 25% position fit the ceiling with a 2% stop. With a 10% stop it breaks it. Change the stop and you must re-run the size.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A1 ceiling, size times stop)

questions.story: A day trade. Your stop is 0.25% under entry, at the low of the first few minutes. You risk 1% of the account, as on your swing trades.
questions.q: How big do you go?
choices: Widen the stop to shrink the size
questions.why: Cap it at 40%, our max. 1 divided by 0.25 is 4, so the formula says 400% of the account. That's four times everything you have, on one day trade. Risk per trade and position size are two separate limits, and you always take the smaller one. Here that's the 40%. A tight stop never earns a giant position. A stop is only a trigger, and a fast market can fill it well below your price. At 400%, a small slip past the stop costs many times the 1% you planned.
questions.lesson_line: A tight stop doesn't license a giant position.

wrong.Buy the full 400%, on margin: A small move the wrong way wipes out a big part of the account. A stop can't save you in a fast market.
wrong.Widen the stop to shrink the size: The stop goes where the trade is wrong. Moving it to fix the size gets it backwards. Change the size instead.
wrong.Tighten the stop even further: A tighter stop makes the formula's size even bigger, and normal noise hits it sooner.

questions.simple: Cap it at 40%, because 1% over a 0.25% stop works out to 400% of the account, way past our max.

deeper.trap: The trap is trusting the formula past its limits. A tight stop makes the formula's size huge, but a stop is only a trigger. A gap or a fast market can fill it well below. At 400% of the account, that loss is many times the 1% you planned.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, A7 40% cap)

questions.q: Day, swing or position trading. Which one do we do most of the time?
choices: Swing, days to a few weeks
Day trades, flat by the close
Position trades, up to a year
A new style for each trade
questions.answer: Swing, days to a few weeks
questions.simple: Swing trades, because we hold for days to a few weeks, and longer only while a winner keeps working.
questions.why: Swing. We hold for days to a few weeks, and a winner can stay on longer as long as it keeps working. That clock is where we catch the real legs without sitting through months of chop. I'd rather ride a few big swings than chase small intraday moves all day. Day trades and position trades still run the same steps you've seen in this lesson. Swing is just our home.
questions.lesson_line: We swing trade. Days to a few weeks, longer only while it works.

wrong.A new style for each trade: We have one home, swing trades, and our plans are built for that clock.
wrong.Day trades, flat by the close: A day trade opens and closes the same day. We hold for days to a few weeks.
wrong.Position trades, up to a year: We don't plan for months. A winner can run longer, but only while it keeps working.

questions.q: Your winner is working, so you decide to hold it longer than you planned. That's no reason to move the stop lower.
questions.simple: True, because the stop only ever moves up. You hold a winner longer by trailing it, not by lowering the stop.
questions.why: True. The stop only moves up, never down or wider. Lower it to give a winner room and you just put back risk you already took off the table. You hold a winner longer by trailing it. Sell some into strength and trail the rest under the rising 9 or 20 EMA. As long as it keeps working, the trail climbs right with it. The only time a stop ever goes lower is a gap down through it, and that's a different spot.
questions.lesson_line: Hold a winner longer with the trail, never by lowering the stop.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, B20 exception)
